title: The Children of Lir
text:
Lir, a lord of the Tuatha De Danann, had four children: a daughter, Fionnuala, and three sons, Aed, Fiachra and Conn. When their mother died, Lir married her sister Aoife. At first she loved the children, but she grew jealous of how much their father and everyone else loved them.

One day she took them to Lough Derravaragh. While they bathed, she struck them with a druid's wand and turned them into four white swans. They kept their human voices and minds. She doomed them to spend three hundred years on that lake, three hundred on the stormy Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland, and three hundred more on the western sea off Inis Gluaire. When Lir learned what had happened, Aoife was punished, but the spell could not be undone.

The nine hundred years were bitter. On the Sea of Moyle the storms were fierce and the cold so harsh that their feet froze to the rocks. Through it all Fionnuala sheltered her brothers: Conn under her right wing, Fiachra under her left, and Aed under the feathers of her breast. She sang to comfort them.

When the spell finally ended, the swans heard a Christian bell. They became human again, but now they were withered, ancient people. A holy man baptized them before they died, and the four were buried together in one grave, as Fionnuala had asked.
lesson: Siblings can carry each other through long hardship. One person who keeps the family together, even in exile, can make it bearable for all.
people: Lir, Aoife, Fionnuala, Aed, Fiachra, Conn
date: late medieval Irish (manuscripts from the 15th century)
source: Oidheadh Chlainne Lir (The Fate of the Children of Lir)
